title: Montaigne's runaway mind
hookLine: idle, his mind bolted like a runaway horse, so he wrote down its fancies to shame it (Essays 1.8)
carry: an idle mind bolts; watch it on paper

cards: The plan was rest. A long weekend, nothing booked, phone on the counter. And by Saturday afternoon the mind has replayed an argument from last spring, drafted a resignation letter, priced a boat, and worried about a mole.

Stillness was supposed to be quiet. Instead it's loud, like a radio left on in an empty house. Montaigne hit exactly this wall right after he climbed into his tower, and he wrote a short essay about it.

teach.b: First, the field. The essay is called Of idleness, and it opens on farmland. A rich field left fallow, he says, doesn't stay empty.
It fills with wild weeds, and to be useful it has to be sown. A mind is the same: leave it with nothing to hold, and it grows its own crop. Second, the horse.
When he retired, Montaigne says, he thought the kindest thing he could do for his mind was to leave it alone, to let it rest and settle into itself. It did the opposite.

teach.h: THE MIND BOLTS LIKE A HORSE.
teach.b: Like a runaway horse, he says, it gave itself a hundred times more free rein than it ever took for anyone else. It bred strange creatures and monsters, one after another, with no order and no point. Third, the trick.
He started writing down what it threw up, so he could look at those odd fancies at leisure. His stated hope was a little sly: that in time, seeing them on paper, his mind would be ashamed of itself.
Fourth, why it matters. Here's a man in a tower with every comfort for thinking, admitting his thinking ran wild.
Some readers find the seed of the whole book in that honesty: in this essay, at least, he says his writing began as notes on a mind that wouldn't sit still.

Off the page, the runaway horse is the three a.m. spiral, or the shower where you win an argument nobody's having. Montaigne's move is plain: don't chase it, write it down, and look at it in daylight.

how: Some readers of Montaigne point to his essay Of idleness as an account of how the Essays began: a restless mind, written down so it could be looked at calmly.

o: a warning that strong feelings must be whipped into line
Montaigne's picture of his idle mind bolting with odd fancies
a picture of a free life with no duties to anyone at all

s: Montaigne says resting in his tower calmed his mind at once
it did the opposite: his mind bolted like a runaway horse.
he says a fallow field fills with wild weeds
a rich field left unsown grows its own crop; so does an idle mind.
Montaigne tried to force his wandering thoughts out
he wrote them down, to look at them at leisure and, he hoped, shame his mind.

games.q: you're Montaigne, newly retired. you left your mind free to rest, and it's running wild with fancies. what do you do?
o: fill every hour with company to drown it out.
start writing the fancies down to look at them.
give up the tower and go back to court.
games.why: he began putting his mind's odd fancies on paper, to study them at leisure and in time make his mind ashamed of itself.

practice: With something to write on nearby, let the horse run, and don't steer it. Each time you notice a thought has carried you off, a worry, a plan, a memory, a song, jot two or three words for it and come back to the breath.
No judging, no fixing: just a list of where the horse went.

wordCard.voice: The runaway horse. Montaigne's picture of his idle mind: left to rest, it bolted and bred fancy after fancy, so he wrote them down to look at in daylight. Today's word.

orig.note: French: a runaway horse, Montaigne's picture of his idle mind.

carryVoice: Your line: an idle mind bolts; watch it on paper. Montaigne's answer was the page, not a tighter rein. Back tomorrow, same hill.
